source: Split the launch velocity into parts, treat each direction on its own, and use the symmetry of the path.
Students think the velocity is zero at the top of the path, forgetting the horizontal part.

A kicked ball, a thrown javelin, a stone from a catapult: each starts with a velocity at an angle. Split it into components, and you have a vertical launch and a steady horizontal motion running side by side, exactly as for a horizontal launch.

Launch at speed $v_0$ and angle $\theta$: $\role[horizontal velocity]{velocity}{v_{0x}} = \role[launch speed]{velocity}{v_0}\cos\role[launch angle]{angle}{\theta}$ stays the same all flight; $\role[vertical launch velocity]{velocity}{v_{0y}} = \role[launch speed]{velocity}{v_0}\sin\role[launch angle]{angle}{\theta}$ changes by $-9.8\ \text{m/s}$ each second. On level ground the path is symmetric: up time equals down time.

Only gravity acts during the flight, and it is vertical. So the vertical motion is a throw straight up with speed $v_{0y}$, and the horizontal motion is steady at $v_{0x}$. At the top only $v_y$ is zero; the ball still moves sideways at $v_{0x}$. For level ground the range is $v_{0x} \times \dfrac{2v_{0y}}{g} = \dfrac{2v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$, which is the same for $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$.
Launched at 20 m/s and 40°, with the 50° path shown dashed: complementary angles give the same range.
A ball is kicked at $20\ \text{m/s}$ at $30^\circ$ above level ground.
Time to the top: $\dfrac{10}{9.8} \approx 1.02\ \text{s}$, so the flight lasts $\approx 2.04\ \text{s}$.
For the same kick, what is the ball's velocity at the top?
From a wall $10\ \text{m}$ high, a ball is thrown at $15\ \text{m/s}$, $40^\circ$ above horizontal. When does it hit the ground?

Saying the velocity is zero at the top of the path. Only the vertical part is zero; the horizontal part is the same as at launch. (Only a ball thrown straight up stops at the top.) Check: at the top, speed $= v_0\cos\theta$, the smallest speed of the flight but not zero.
Try it in the Science Lab's Trebuchet Workshop: change the release angle and see the range. With air drag, the best angle drops a little below $45^\circ$.
